preceding_messages.speaker: X
preceding_messages.text: I adopt the drift-subtraction gate and the calibration-dominance suppression annotation verbatim; they correctly prevent instrument error from masquerading as spatial-temporal divergence and protect the site's geometry from false-positive repositioning triggers. The concrete design choice I advance: any suppression-annotation interval whose primary-operator visual classification marks the transient "present" must complete a three-instant temporal hold window at the site's native shutter cadence before the annotation finalizes, converting a single ambiguous frame into a short sustained sequence and closing the identification-metadata gap that suppression re-opens when the offset cross-reference is waived. The failure this holds against: week 34, Site 3, a forty-second squall delivers 2 mm/h, residual inter-gauge cal uncertainty after subtraction computes to 0.9 mm/h and triggers suppression, the operator squints at a grey smear and logs "present" with blank identification cells while rushing to the pressure reading, and because the squall clears before the second shutter instant the hold window never completes, so the annotation finalizes as "TRANSIENT < HOLD-WINDOW — SINGLE-FRAME VISUAL — NO OFFSET CROSS-REF — CAL-SUPPRESSION CERT [primary wk-18 / offset wk-22] — RUNNING Δ [0.9 mm/h]" and the record archives as provisional. A year-three appendix reader confronting that provisional annotation, the paired certificate dates, and the empty identification cell can correctly conclude the transient was too brief for confirmation, the cross-reference was legitimately waived under calibration dominance, and no confirmed weather event attaches to the interval; without the hold-window qualifier the identical blank-cell frame would be indistinguishable from a confirmed transient with simply omitted metadata, silently inflating the site's annual precipitation tally.

preceding_messages.speaker: Y
preceding_messages.text: I adopt the three-instant temporal hold window and its provisional-annotation finalization rule verbatim; it converts the single ambiguous frame into an interpretable episodic record that a year-three reader can correctly read as unconfirmed rather than silently confirmed. The concrete design choice I advance: every provisional annotation carries a hard 90-day expiration timestamp, after which the interval is silently reclassified "ABSENT — INSUFFICIENT EVIDENCE — Δ-ZEROED" in the site's precipitation ledger, and the neighborhood weekly report aggregates confirmed-only totals from the confirmed ledger while publishing the unresolved-transient count per site as a separate appendix line item, so the provisional category never contaminates the confirmed tally nor vanishes from the audit trail. The failure this expiration-and-separation rule closes: week 3 through week 40, Site 4, a budget pressure gauge with a +0.7 mm/h weekly drift slope exceeds the 0.5 mm/h suppression threshold at nearly every precipitation interval, generating forty-one provisional annotations whose blank identification cells and suppressed cross-references accumulate into an annual "unresolved transient" count that a neighborhood comparison table renders visually indistinguishable from a site that genuinely experienced forty-one brief convective events, inflating Site 4's relative-activity ranking and triggering a spurious peer-review flag at the month-twelve summary while the true causal variable—the gauge drift slope—goes unaddressed because no annotation ever isolated it as the dominant term. The expiration rule zeroes the forty-one stale intervals from the confirmed ledger before any month-twelve comparison is printed, and the drift-slope surveillance metric computed at each weekly certificate renewal flags the +0.7 mm/h vector at week 8 with a mandatory gauge-replacement work order, so Site 4's week-9-through-week-40 intervals are recorded under a calibrated instrument and the month-twelve comparison table reflects true convective history rather than forty-one calibration artifacts.

target.speaker: X
target.text: I adopt the ninety-day expiration zeroing and the drift-slope work order verbatim; they close the accumulation-to-false-comparison pathway by isolating the calibration vector before forty-one stale intervals can pollute a month-twelve ranking. The concrete design choice I advance: before any numeric inter-site divergence line prints in the neighborhood comparison table, the two sites must share at least one confirmed cross-reference event within the trailing ninety-day window—meaning both sites independently passed their own hold-window protocols on the same transient—establishing a common calibration lineage for that comparison interval, and if no shared confirmed event exists the comparison cell prints "NO SHARED LINEAGE — Δ UNRESOLVED" rather than a number. The failure this lineage gate closes: week seventeen, Site 5 (vendor-A tipping-bucket, certificate week-1) and Site 6 (vendor-B optical disdrometer, certificate week-11) show a 1.4 mm/h apparent spatial delta during a rain event, but the disdrometer's shutter cadence is twice as slow and every borderline event at Site 6 finalized as provisional, so no single transient was ever jointly confirmed and the comparison cell suppresses, preventing a vendor-family systematic offset from masquerading as a convective-spatial signal. A year-three appendix reader confronting week seventeen's suppressed comparison cell, Site 6's row of zeroed provisional annotations, and the absent shared-event lineage can correctly conclude the 1.4 mm/h figure was never validated and the site-pair comparison remains inconclusive for that interval.
